It was the second most targeted skill across reviewed programmes.

name: SEL skills: self-management
description: Sreekala, Bender and Day (2025) name self-management, the most targeted SEL skill, encompassing emotion regulation, stress management, coping skills, goal setting and self-regulation.

name: SEL skills: relationship skills
description: Sreekala, Bender and Day (2025) name relationship skills as an SEL domain covering relationship-building, social skills, communication, cooperation and social connectedness.

name: Certification and qualification pathways
description: Falk et al. (2019) describe how training by non-governmental actors often does not lead to certification, leaving teachers without formal recognition and unable to work in national systems, and call for sustained in-service training culminating in recognised certification.

name: Predictable school routines and rituals
description: Burde et al. (2015) describe regular school routines and rituals that provide crisis-affected children with a component of normal life, an anchor and a sense of consistency, supporting mental health and resilience.

name: Sustained attendance and time-in-school supports
description: Palik and Østby (2023) describe interventions that keep children in school more consistently, such as cash transfers covering commuting costs and foregone income that raise days and time in school, and monitoring that increases pupil presence.

name: Education management information systems (EMIS) and policy coordination
description: Pherali and Rinehart (2026) describe system-level strengthening through education management information systems (EMIS) and aligned policy and coordination that embed displaced learners in host-country data and provision, an area flagged as a major evidence and implementation gap.

name: Guided play-based classroom pedagogy
description: Kwok, Sable and Smiley (2026) define learning through play integrated into curriculum delivery, where an adult facilitator uses playful instruction and active, student-centred practices, as in the PlayMatters teacher professional development programme.

name: Child-friendly spaces and play hubs
description: Kwok, Sable and Smiley (2026) describe non-formal spaces combining guided play, games and foundational content (singing, drawing, recreation, life skills, literacy, non-violent conflict resolution), delivered by trained community facilitators, for example Child Friendly Spaces and Humanitarian Play Labs.

name: Structured recreational and psychosocial play activities
description: Kwok, Sable and Smiley (2026) define play-based child-facing content delivered outside curriculum to target specific competencies, using movement games, songs, breathing and cooperative games, for example Psychosocial Structured Activities and TeamUp.

name: Water and sanitation infrastructure
description: Bick et al. (2025) describe water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) hardware in schools, spanning water quantity and quality (points, treatment, safe storage) and sanitation (latrine construction, often gender-segregated, plus cleaning and privacy), finding effects on illness absence and attendance heterogeneous.

name: Hygiene promotion and behaviour change
description: Bick et al. (2025) describe handwashing facilities, soap or sanitiser combined with behaviour-change promotion (hygiene education, play-based approaches, nudges, hygiene clubs) to establish handwashing with soap, reporting mixed impacts on illness and absence.

name: Menstrual health management
description: Bick et al. (2025) describe provision of private, secure, gender-segregated toilets and washing facilities enabling girls to manage menstruation, noting that no included interventions supplied menstrual materials or education, a marked evidence gap; Psaki et al. (2022) rate the menstrual-hygiene evidence as insufficient.

name: Multi-tiered school-based support matching intensity to need
description: Sullivan and Simonson (2016) describe a school-linked model where treatment intensity is individualised by severity across tiers, for example community psychoeducation, weekly skill-building groups, trauma systems therapy for referred children, and intensive home-based therapy for the severely impaired, with movement between tiers by assessed need.

name: Multi-layered MHPSS system of care (IASC pyramid)
description: Jordans, Pigott and Tol (2016) describe a whole-system approach delivering support across levels, from population-wide humanitarian support, to non-specialised activities strengthening family and community protective factors, to focused non-specialised care, up to specialised services for the smaller share with significant distress, with screening used to route children upward.

name: Positive-discipline and anti-corporal-punishment teacher training
description: Kagan and Fabbri (2026) describe behaviourally informed teacher training (for example EmpaTeach) using empathy-building and self-regulation techniques, positive disciplinary methods and classroom-management strategies to reduce corporal punishment, noting stand-alone training did not reduce violence without wider school engagement and norm change.

name: Personal-safety education for pupils
description: Kagan and Fabbri (2026) describe a school-based personal-safety curriculum (for example Be Safe) teaching young children about safe and unsafe touching, children's rights, adults' protection duties and supportive friendships, which improved children's ability to recognise and report violence and raised perceived safety.

name: Safe reporting and referral pathways
description: Parkes et al. (2016) and Kagan and Fabbri (2026) describe reporting and referral systems and case management that give children a safe route to disclose violence and be linked to child-protection, health or welfare services, requiring functioning links between schools and external services.

name: Whole-school violence prevention that changes rules and relationships
description: Parkes et al. (2016) describe engaging the whole school community, including leadership, in developing and sustaining policies, protocols and practices that reduce violence and promote non-violent, equitable norms, finding this more effective than isolated classroom sessions.

name: School codes of conduct and accountability mechanisms
description: Parkes et al. (2016) describe formal teacher codes of conduct and accountability systems that define prohibited behaviour and ensure teachers found guilty of offences are sanctioned rather than transferred, noting gaps where guidelines lack legal force, distribution or training.

name: Accelerated education programmes (AEP)
description: Burde et al. (2015) describe accelerated education programmes (AEP), also called catch-up education or open schools, designed for over-age out-of-school youth, condensing roughly eight years of primary schooling into three to four years.

name: Child and youth learning centres and catch-up clubs
description: Palik and Østby (2023) describe community-based child and youth learning centres for out-of-school children, including camp settings, providing non-formal learning that improves literacy and numeracy.

name: Peace education and intergroup contact
description: Burde et al. (2015) describe peace education and intergroup contact bringing together learners from different groups to build positive attitudes, finding short-term attitude gains and warning that one-sided negative history can reinforce conflict. Pherali and Rinehart (2026) report a perspective-taking and intergroup curriculum in Turkey that reduced peer violence, victimisation and segregation and increased interethnic links.

name: Contextualised and co-designed digital content
description: Barnes and Katrin (2025) describe education technology (EdTech) content designed collaboratively with displaced communities and localised to their language, curriculum, characters and context, as in Can't Wait to Learn co-creation workshops, rather than off-the-shelf material.

name: Adaptive, self-directed and gamified learning apps
description: Barnes and Katrin (2025) describe gamified applications for autonomous, self-paced practice that adapt difficulty and give instant feedback and rewards, such as Akelius, Feed the Monster and EduApp4Syria.

name: Tablet and mobile device learning
description: Barnes and Katrin (2025) describe provision of portable devices such as tablets and mobile phones to deliver learning content usable offline and immediately on arrival, harnessing the technology most available to displaced populations.

name: Radio and audio instruction
description: Crompton et al. (2021) describe delivery of lessons through non-internet audio channels such as radio and interactive audio, a low-tech system usable where connectivity and devices are scarce.

name: Teacher training for inclusive education
description: Hunt et al. (2025) describe programmes and policy that build teachers' capacity to educate learners with a wide range of needs, including disability-awareness training and inclusive-education pedagogy, promising when accompanied by appropriate materials and school-level support.

name: Targeted and assistive learner-level supports
description: Hunt et al. (2025) describe individual-level interventions equipping learners with disabilities for formal learning (reading-comprehension strategy instruction, early literacy and numeracy) plus rehabilitation, health services and assistive technologies such as wheelchairs and devices.

name: Twin-track provision
description: Hunt et al. (2025) describe a combined approach that simultaneously addresses the specific individual needs of children with disabilities and ensures they are included in mainstream activities, rather than only individual functioning or only environmental reform.

name: System and school-level inclusive reform
description: Hunt et al. (2025) describe institutional changes such as implementing inclusive-education policy, making the built environment and materials accessible through universal design, and school-wide anti-bullying policies, so children are mainstreamed rather than merely housed in schools; evidence here is thinner than for targeted supports.

name: Teacher social-emotional learning and stress management
description: Berger et al. (2022) find most evaluated educator-wellbeing initiatives are individual therapeutic programmes (mindfulness, social and emotional learning (SEL), mental-health literacy, cognitive-behavioural, positive-psychology), which mostly improved teacher stress and wellbeing. Falk et al. (2019) define teacher social-emotional competence via five competencies that buffer stress and burnout.

name: Supportive leadership and collaboration time
description: Falk et al. (2019) identify supportive leadership and peer collaboration as school-level protective factors, where supportive leaders foster a culture of trust and care, though collaboration becomes a stressor when inadequate time is provided. Berger et al. (2022) add a school-leadership and policy-change category targeting participative decision-making.

name: Manageable workload and class size
description: Falk et al. (2019) name workload and large class sizes as major stressors, citing settings with student-teacher ratios over 160 to 1 and multi-subject, multi-grade loads that leave teachers ill-equipped and undermine wellbeing. Berger et al. (2022) note initiatives rarely address these systemic workplace demands.

name: Digital data systems to locate and track displaced learners
description: Barnes and Katrin (2025) describe technology-enabled data tools that collect and analyse information to locate displaced students and monitor their enrolment and needs, for example a refugee-data application for the UN High Commissioner for Refugees.

name: Displacement-disaggregated targeting and differential-effect monitoring
description: Pherali and Rinehart (2026) and Palik and Østby (2023) describe designing and monitoring provision for internally displaced, refugee and host learners separately and tracking differential effects, so equity gaps such as a widening numeracy gap between host and displaced learners are detected.

name: Mother-tongue or home-language instruction
description: Pherali and Rinehart (2026) describe teaching displaced and language-minority children in their home or first language to support identity, belonging and foundational learning, as distinct from instruction in a dominant or official language.

name: Host or second-language acquisition support
description: Pherali and Rinehart (2026) describe targeted instruction that builds proficiency in the official or host-community language of schooling, for example Healing Classrooms remedial literacy in French and Turkish-language programmes for Arabic- and Kurdish-speaking refugees.

name: Bilingual accelerated or remedial curriculum
description: Pherali and Rinehart (2026) describe a time-bound accelerated or catch-up curriculum taught by facilitators fluent in both the host language and learners' first language, such as a 10-week bilingual pre-primary accelerated curriculum in Turkey.

name: Visual and creative arts therapy
description: Noyes, Kubishyn and Brown (2025) classify visual arts as a creative expressive therapy using practices such as painting and drawing, delivered by trained art therapists in school or community settings.

name: Drama and theatre
description: Noyes, Kubishyn and Brown (2025) include theatre as a creative expressive therapy delivered by drama therapists in school settings.

name: Music
description: Noyes, Kubishyn and Brown (2025) include music as a creative expressive therapy in which children make themselves heard non-verbally through instruments, delivered by music therapists.

name: Narrative and expressive writing
description: Sreekala, Bender and Day (2025) describe creative-expression programmes in which youth create trauma narratives through writing, such as Writing for Recovery, and storytelling and drawing to integrate cultural identity and migration experiences.

name: Centre-based early childhood development for school readiness
description: Burde et al. (2015) describe centre-based early childhood development (ECD) or preschool provision delivering early stimulation and building early language, literacy, numeracy and cognitive skills, improving readiness for and transition into primary school.

name: ECD for refugee second-language acquisition
description: Palik and Østby (2023) describe enrolling newly arrived refugee children in early childhood development programmes as a stage for acquiring the host-country language and easing transition to school.

name: Provision and availability of basic learning materials
description: Snilstveit et al. (2015) define materials-provision interventions as any intervention providing traditional hardware materials such as textbooks, chalkboards or other classroom equipment, addressing supply-side determinants of educational quality.

name: Classroom use of materials in lessons
description: Snilstveit et al. (2015) stress that provision improves outcomes only when teachers distribute and use materials in lessons and allocate sufficient time to their use. The driver is observed use, distinct from mere availability.

name: Localised, low-cost, level-appropriate materials
description: Kaffenberger et al. (2026) specify materials that are localised, low cost and well aligned with the progression of literacy and numeracy goals, providing a range of instructional materials catering to different learning levels.

name: Learner-centred pedagogy (active learner control)
description: Bremner, Sakata and Cameron (2023), citing Schweisfurth, define learner-centred pedagogy as an approach giving learners a relatively high level of active control over the content and process of learning, with more active learning, adaptation to learner needs, greater autonomy and reduced teacher-learner power distance.

name: Interactive, activity-based instruction (learning by doing)
description: Kaffenberger et al. (2026) describe interactive techniques where pupils work in groups and use paired reading, gamified activities and manipulatives, emphasising learning through doing, practice, discussion and application over passive knowledge acquisition.

name: Dialogic and student-led talk
description: Kaffenberger et al. (2026) include as an interactive technique students leading activities and group discussions in front of the whole class, making classroom talk a two-way, pupil-led process rather than teacher transmission.

name: Community mobilisation and participation in school management
description: Burde et al. (2015) describe involving local communities in education provision through management training, parent associations and seed grants that give parents a role in running schools, motivating demand and enrolment.

name: Participatory community monitoring of schools
description: Burde et al. (2015) describe an enhanced participatory model where school management committees design their own instruments to monitor teachers and pupils, increasing collective action and accountability, as distinct from top-down monitoring.

name: Universal classroom SEL and stress-reduction programme
description: Bangpan et al. (2024) describe a universal school-based programme delivered to every child in a class that pairs stress-reduction strategies with pro-social strategies such as perspective-taking, empathy and mindfulness, run by a teacher or trained facilitator and not conditional on a symptom screen.

name: Classroom-based structured psychosocial and recreational activities
description: Tyrer and Fazel (2014) describe structured group activities using drama, music, drawing, games and sport to build relationships, expression and wellbeing, delivered in schools to all enrolled children by trained non-specialist facilitators, aiming at promotion of wellbeing rather than symptom treatment.

name: Selective classroom intervention blending creative-expressive and CBT elements
description: Arega (2023) describes a selective, preventive classroom programme structured on creative-expressive plus cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT) concepts (safety, stabilisation, trauma narrative, coping, reconnection), targeting children screened for elevated distress and facilitated by trained local volunteers who are mostly schoolteachers.

name: Teacher capacity-building for a supportive classroom climate
description: Arega (2023) describes training that strengthens teachers' skills in emotional communication and in creating an emotionally safe classroom, so the class teacher, not an outside clinician, becomes the vehicle for psychosocial support, acting on children indirectly.

name: School-leader management training and support
description: Anand et al. (2023) describe training, professional development and workshops that build the managerial and instructional-leadership skills of principals and head teachers, often paired with school-improvement plans, performance information, feedback or coaching and materials.

name: In-school meals (breakfast, lunch or snacks)
description: Wang et al. (2021) describe the provision of food or beverages consumed at school (meals or snacks, centrally or school-prepared), finding it improves attendance and anthropometry more consistently than learning.

name: Take-home rations
description: Wang et al. (2021) treat take-home rations as a distinct feeding modality: food distributed to households conditional on the child's enrolment and consumed outside school, intended to offset the household cost of schooling while improving nutrition.

name: Complementary micronutrient, deworming and health measures
description: Wang et al. (2021) describe deworming, nutrition or health education and micronutrient provision delivered as complements to feeding, finding no significant pooled effect on micronutrient status, so nutrition and attendance gains are more consistent than blood-nutrient or learning gains.

name: Community-based education (community and village schools)
description: Burde et al. (2015) describe establishing schools within the community itself, supported and managed through community participation, to provide primary education where infrastructure is weak and government schools are distant, increasing access (especially for girls) and raising achievement.

name: Subject-focused, practice-based training
description: Popova et al. (2022) find professional development focused on subject-specific pedagogy produces larger learning gains, with no-subject-focus programmes showing 0.24 standard deviations lower impact. Effective training is concrete and classroom-based rather than theoretical.

name: Rehearsal and enactment of lessons in training
description: Popova et al. (2022) define lesson enactment as teachers practising lessons during the training; a programme with lesson enactment is associated with a 0.10 standard deviation increase in student learning. It gives teachers hands-on rehearsal of the lessons they will deliver.

name: Video-supported reflection
description: Hennessy et al. (2022) describe video-based self-reflective professional development where teachers record and watch lessons to evaluate their own practice and view expert modelling, most effective when paired with structured reflection, questioning and discussion.

name: Social-messaging and peer teacher communities
description: Hennessy et al. (2022) describe low-cost messaging (Short Message Service, WhatsApp, Facebook groups) used to support, prompt or reinforce new teacher practices through reminders, accountability nudges and peer exchange, cautioning that messaging alone cannot provide the observation and feedback elements of coaching.

name: Professional development linked to career incentives
description: Popova et al. (2022) find linking participation to career opportunities (promotion, salary or status) is robustly associated with higher gains; where participation has no such implication, student learning is 0.12 standard deviations lower.

name: Gender-norm and attitude-change curricula
description: Kagan and Fabbri (2026) and Parkes et al. (2016) describe structured lessons on gendered interactions, norms and relationships designed to shift gender attitudes and reduce acceptance of violence, for example an Afghanistan whole-school peace-education and social-norms programme that improved gender and non-violence attitudes.

name: Engaging boys and men
description: Kagan and Fabbri (2026) describe group sessions with male youth (for example Young Men Initiative) using reflection on masculinity, gender attitudes, violence and health to promote non-violent, gender-equitable masculinity. North and Ozawa (2026) identify the lack of attention to boys and men as a significant gap.

name: Community gender sensitisation and dialogue
description: North and Ozawa (2026) and Parkes et al. (2016) describe engagement with parents and community and religious gatekeepers, including whole-community approaches, to challenge norms that underpin gender-based violence (GBV) and restrict girls' schooling, finding school-based norm work has limited impact where not linked to community engagement.

name: Gender-sensitive facilities and environment
description: Psaki et al. (2022) describe construction and improvement of school facilities, especially single-sex toilets, handwashing stations and safe latrines, to reduce a gender-insensitive environment as a participation barrier, rating water and sanitation improvements, especially toilets, as a promising approach for girls.

name: Girls' scholarships and financial support
description: Psaki et al. (2022) rate interventions addressing tuition and fees as effective and school materials as promising, and North and Ozawa (2026) find cash transfers and scholarships improve girls' access as part of holistic strategies. The driver removes the inability to afford schooling as a gender-related barrier.

name: Girls' empowerment through clubs, mentoring and safe spaces
description: North and Ozawa (2026) describe girls' empowerment through clubs, mentoring and safe spaces that build awareness of gender equality, life skills and social connections, reporting promising norm shifts when combined with other interventions; Psaki et al. (2022) rate the evidence on safe spaces as inconclusive and under-examined.

name: Regular assessment to identify current learning levels
description: Kaffenberger et al. (2026) define Teaching at the Right Level (TaRL) assessment as simple, repeated testing used to establish baseline learning levels, assign children to groups, and regroup as learning changes. The driver is the ongoing assess-and-regroup process.

name: Grouping and aligning instruction to learning level
description: Kaffenberger et al. (2026) state that once assessed, instruction is aligned to each child's current learning level, typically by grouping children who score similarly and teaching to the level of each group, rather than by age or grade.

name: Focus on a streamlined set of foundational skills
description: Kaffenberger et al. (2026) say TaRL programmes identify and focus on a narrow set of foundational literacy and numeracy skills, dedicating instructional time to mastery of those targeted skills.

name: Trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy (TF-CBT)
description: Sullivan and Simonson (2016) describe TF-CBT as a targeted, manualised trauma treatment sequencing psychoeducation, relaxation, affective modulation, cognitive coping, a trauma narrative and safety planning, usually delivered by clinicians (some manuals for trained non-specialists) to screened, symptomatic children individually or in small groups.

name: Narrative exposure therapy (NET / KIDNET)
description: Bangpan et al. (2024) describe a short individual trauma treatment in which the child, with a trained therapist, constructs a chronological lifeline of traumatic and positive events and revisits selected memories to build a coherent narrative and reduce symptoms (KIDNET is the child-adapted form).

name: Group interpersonal psychotherapy (GIPT)
description: Jordans, Pigott and Tol (2016) describe a group therapy targeting depression and interpersonal difficulties, focused on relationship triggers and group relationships, delivered by trained non-specialists to screened, distressed youth, with effects varying by subgroup.

name: Group psychosocial support counselling
description: Arega (2023) describes group counselling for war-exposed pupils led by trained school counsellors, social workers and teachers, provided to children referred or identified as more affected, to reduce traumatic stress and functional impairment. It is school-based but targeted rather than universal.

name: Individual counselling
description: Jordans, Pigott and Tol (2016) describe one-to-one counselling by a non-specialist counsellor centred on trust and disclosure, active problem solving, structured trauma-focused exposure and family involvement, with effects depending on the counsellor relationship and undermined by a moralistic stance.

name: Implementation quality: facilitation, contextual adaptation and dosage
description: Barnes and Katrin (2025), with corroboration across the review set, describe cross-cutting moderators of effect, namely trained human facilitation, adaptation of content to local context, and the dose or intensity of delivery, which shape whether tools and programmes actually work.

name: Structured parenting-education programmes
description: Lee and Kim (2022) describe parenting-education programmes delivering education, information or expert lectures with counselling, training and mentoring to produce positive changes in parenting attitudes and behaviours among refugee and migrant parents.

name: Family-strengthening and caregiver-support programmes
description: Gillespie et al. (2022) describe structured activities engaging caregivers directly to influence parenting behaviours such as nurturing, discipline, teaching, monitoring and management, often as family-based group programmes for displaced families.

name: Caregiver wellbeing and psychological support
description: Västhagen et al. (2026) describe psychosocial interventions designed to enhance resilience and support parents in the parental role while reducing parental psychological distress (depression, anxiety, stress and trauma-related symptoms) among forced-migrant parents.

name: Teaching presence in remote learning
description: Pacitto et al. (2026) describe deliberate practices that maintain a visible, active teacher role during remote instruction through regular contact, structuring and guidance, consistently linked with stronger outcomes than passive content distribution.

name: Two-way interaction and feedback
description: Pacitto et al. (2026) describe structured channels for formative feedback between teacher and learner, and from learners and caregivers back to teachers and decision-makers, linked to stronger learning and social-emotional outcomes than one-way delivery.

name: Facilitated peer and group remote learning
description: Pacitto et al. (2026) describe organising remote learners into structured groups or peer forums, often convened by a community-based facilitator, which raised the effectiveness of radio and short-message lessons, as in Kenya's girls' reading camps.

name: Caregiver-supported remote learning
description: Pacitto et al. (2026) describe enabling caregivers to act as at-home facilitators of remote learning through clear roles and regular nudges, especially for primary-age children, as in interactive-audio trials in Bangladesh.

name: Multimodal, blended synchronous-asynchronous delivery
description: Pacitto et al. (2026) describe combining live synchronous and pre-recorded or paper-based asynchronous modes, and internet with non-internet channels, tailored by education stage and connectivity to sustain access and engagement.

name: Teacher coaching (observation-and-feedback cycle)
description: Kraft, Blazar and Hogan (2018) define coaching as all in-service programmes where coaches or peers observe teachers' instruction and provide feedback, centred on an observation and feedback cycle. They specify it as individualised, intensive (at least every couple of weeks), sustained, situated in the teacher's own classroom, and focused on discrete skills, which distinguishes it from short generalised workshops.

name: Teacher mentoring (out-of-classroom guidance for new teachers)
description: Kraft, Blazar and Hogan (2018) treat mentoring as distinct from coaching and exclude induction mentoring, noting a mentor's role differs from a coach's and may cover work-life balance and interaction with school leadership, situated outside the classroom. Mentoring pairs a novice with an experienced colleague for career and socialisation support rather than a classroom observation cycle.

name: Communities of practice and teacher learning circles
description: Falk et al. (2019), citing Wenger, define communities of practice as learning networks that encourage teachers to share knowledge, resources and ideas to continually develop their teaching, which can be formal (Teacher Learning Circles) or informal peer help.

name: Virtual or remote coaching
description: Kraft, Blazar and Hogan (2018) describe virtual coaching where teachers record their own teaching and discuss it with a virtual coach on a web platform, finding no significant difference from in-person coaching. Hennessy et al. (2022) add that it involves observing, modelling, supporting and offering focused personalised feedback iteratively by video conferencing.

name: Lesson observation and structured feedback
description: Kraft, Blazar and Hogan (2018) anchor coaching in the observation-and-feedback cycle where instructional experts discuss classroom practice in the teacher's own classroom, rated on defined instruments. Hennessy et al. (2022) show technology can strengthen this through guided observation protocols and generated feedback.

name: Scripted or semi-scripted lesson plans
description: Snilstveit et al. (2015) describe structured pedagogy as programmes that pre-specify what and how teachers teach by developing structured lesson content and evidence-based curricula, content and lesson plans. The driver is the structured plan itself, separate from its delivery.

name: Teacher training on delivering the structured lessons
description: In Snilstveit et al. (2015), structured pedagogy provides teachers with training in delivering the material so they gain the knowledge and skills to deliver new content, typically through short-term training courses tied to the lessons.

name: Ongoing in-classroom support and supervision within the package
description: Snilstveit et al. (2015) include ongoing teacher support, supervision and feedback after initial training so teachers adopt and sustain the new classroom practices. This is the follow-up layer of the structured pedagogy package.

name: Teacher and pupil materials matched to the structured lessons
description: In Snilstveit et al. (2015), structured pedagogy provides materials for both teachers and children, including teacher guides and classroom learning materials designed to accompany the structured lesson content. This is materials matched to the scripts, not generic provision.

name: Conditional cash transfers (CCT)
description: Baird et al. (2013) define conditional cash transfers (CCT) as cash payments to households contingent on required schooling behaviours such as a minimum attendance level, raising income and lowering the price of schooling, with the transfer paid only when the condition is met.

name: Unconditional cash transfers (UCT)
description: Baird et al. (2013) define unconditional cash transfers (UCT) as cash payments to poor households with no strings attached, acting solely through an income effect, paid regardless of behaviour.

name: Monitoring and enforcement of schooling conditions
description: Baird et al. (2013) place programmes on a continuum from unconditional to fully enforced conditional, finding CCT and UCT do not differ significantly overall but explicitly monitored and enforced conditions produce the largest effect. They code this intensity from zero to six.

name: Scholarships, fee subsidies and vouchers
description: Burde et al. (2015) describe in-kind or targeted subsidies that reduce the direct cost of schooling, for example vouchers covering part of private-school fees or per-pupil subsidies to enrol children in local private schools, on the theory that removing cost barriers restores access.

name: Cash-plus and social marketing of schooling value
description: Baird et al. (2013) describe cash bundled with educational encouragement, community meetings or media that prime the value of schooling, noting UCT arms were more effective than CCT arms at preventing teen pregnancy and marriage, a girls' wellbeing trade-off.

name: Pay teachers in full and on time
description: Pay teachers in full and on time

description: Recognise displaced teachers' qualifications

name: Provide sustained certified in-service training
description: Provide sustained certified in-service training

name: Offer teacher scholarships and advancement
description: Offer teacher scholarships and advancement

name: Coordinate policy for displaced learners
description: Coordinate policy for displaced learners

name: Screen children and refer to appropriate care
